passage: At the milk cooperative office in a small Maharashtra town, Irawati watched Parveen snap at the weighing clerk over a missing sticker, something she had never done in four years. Twice that week the ledger showed wrong totals, and Parveen no longer joined the tea circle at eleven. Irawati said nothing in front of the others. Instead, after closing on Thursday, she asked, "Walk with me to the bus stop?" On the way she said, "You have seemed worn out lately. I am not asking for details, only whether I can take the Saturday totals off you." Parveen's eyes filled, and she nodded. Irawati checked the totals, and the next Monday she said that if the tiredness kept going or worried her, it was worth seeing a doctor.

qa.q: Where did Irawati ask Parveen to walk with her?
qa.a: Irawati asked Parveen to walk with her to the bus stop after closing on Thursday.

qa.q: What might Irawati have been feeling when she noticed Parveen snapping and making errors?
qa.a: Concerned and careful, which is why she chose to speak privately.

qa.q: Why was the walk to the bus stop a better choice than a remark in the tea circle?
qa.a: A private, caring word avoids embarrassing Parveen in front of others and makes it easier to accept help.

qa.q: What is it like for Parveen when Irawati offers to take the Saturday totals?
qa.a: A relief and an emotional moment; Parveen's eyes fill, which shows she was carrying more than she said.

grounding: Illustrates a coworker noticing irritability, careless errors and withdrawal and offering a private check-in and a suggestion to see a doctor.

passage: Ingrid noticed it first on the tram: Priscila, usually chatty, stared out of the window with her headphones on. In the office the pattern grew. Priscila corrected a colleague with a sharp sigh at Tuesday's meeting, sent a report with the wrong month in the title and ate lunch alone at her desk. Ingrid did not raise it in the group chat. On Friday she wrote, "Coffee downstairs at three? No agenda." Over the cups she said, "You seem stretched thin. I am not judging." Priscila was quiet, then said she had not slept well for weeks. Ingrid mentioned the company's confidential support line and offered to sit with her while she called.

qa.q: What was wrong with the report Priscila sent?
qa.a: The report had the wrong month in the title.

qa.q: What might Ingrid have been feeling as she chose not to raise it in the group chat?
qa.a: Concerned and careful, wanting to protect Priscila's dignity.

qa.q: What could Priscila do if the poor sleep keeps going?
qa.a: Call the confidential support line, with Ingrid beside her, or check with a doctor.

qa.q: What is it like for Priscila to be invited for coffee with no agenda?
qa.a: Probably a relief and less pressure than being called out in a group; she was quiet at first, then opened up about her sleep.

grounding: Illustrates a coworker noticing irritability, careless errors and withdrawal and choosing a private check-in and pointing to professional support.

passage:
At the bank branch, Rashmi had sat next to Jahnavi for two years. Jahnavi was usually the one who remembered birthdays and hummed while counting cash.
Over three weeks, Rashmi noticed a change. Jahnavi snapped at a customer about a form. She made two counting errors in one day, which had never happened. At lunch, she ate at her desk and didn't join the others.
In the Monday meeting, the manager said, "Some of us need to be more careful with the counting." Everyone looked at Jahnavi. Rashmi saw her face close.
That evening Rashmi waited until everyone had left. "Jahnavi, want to get chai? Just us."
At the stall, Rashmi said, "You don't seem like yourself lately. I'm not asking to fix anything. Just checking."
Jahnavi's eyes filled. Her mother was ill; she had been at the hospital every night.
Before they left, Rashmi gave her the number of the bank's employee counselling line and offered to cover her counter on Thursday afternoon.

qa.q: How many counting errors did Jahnavi make in one day?
qa.a: She made two counting errors in one day.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she saw Jahnavi's face close in the meeting?
qa.a: Rashmi felt concerned and protective, sensing the public remark had hurt Jahnavi.

qa.q: Why was the chai check-in better than the manager's comment?
qa.a: It was private and caring, asking without judging, so Jahnavi could share what was happening and get support.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt when Rashmi asked, "Just checking"?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably felt relieved and moved, finally able to say how hard things had been.

grounding: An observer notices a colleague becoming irritable, error-prone and withdrawn, and chooses a private, caring check-in and points to counselling.

passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
I hope it's okay that I'm writing this instead of saying it at work. I didn't want to say it in front of anyone.
I've noticed you've been having a hard few weeks. You used to join us for lunch, and lately you eat at your desk. You snapped at the intern on Friday, which isn't like you at all. And the invoice mix-up last week, I know that's not you either.
I'm not writing to point at any of that. I'm writing because I care how you're doing.
If you ever want to take a walk after work, I'm around. No need to explain anything.
And if it's been heavy for a while, our company has a counselling service that's confidential. I used it last year when my father was ill, and it helped me more than I expected. The number is on the HR noticeboard.
Either way, I'm on your side.
Gurpreet

qa.q: Where does Elizabeth eat lunch lately?
qa.a: Lately you eat at your desk.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet seem to feel about Elizabeth's changes?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels concerned and caring, wanting to reach out without embarrassing Elizabeth.

qa.q: Why was a private letter a good choice here?
qa.a: It let Gurpreet show care without a public remark, offer company and point gently to confidential counselling.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Elizabeth might feel surprised and a little exposed at first, but also relieved that someone noticed kindly.

grounding: An observer colleague notices someone withdrawing, snapping and making errors, and offers a private, caring check-in and professional support.

passage:
You asked on the podcast about looking out for colleagues. I'm Raghav, and I'll tell you about Irawati.
She was the sharpest person in our team. Then, over about a month, she changed. She went quiet in meetings. She made two mistakes in the client report, small ones, but she never made mistakes. When someone joked about it, she snapped and left the room.
Our manager said in the team chat, "Please double-check before sending." Everyone knew who it was for.
I didn't want to do that. So I messaged her privately: "Coffee downstairs at four? No agenda."
She came. I said, "You seem really tired lately. I'm not asking for a reason. Just asking how you are." She stared at her cup for a long time, then said she hadn't slept properly in weeks and didn't know why.
I told her about the company's counsellor, and I walked her to HR the next morning to get the number. She went. She's better now, slowly.

qa.q: What time did Raghav suggest for coffee?
qa.a: Coffee downstairs at four.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel about the manager's message in the team chat?
qa.a: Raghav felt uncomfortable with it, not wanting to point at Irawati in public.

qa.q: What did Raghav do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: Raghav invited Irawati privately, asked how she was without demanding a reason, and walked her to HR to get the counsellor's number, which made support easy to reach.

qa.q: How did Irawati seem to feel at the coffee?
qa.a: Irawati seemed exhausted and unsure, staring at her cup before admitting she hadn't slept properly in weeks.

grounding: An observer notices a colleague withdrawing and making errors, checks in privately and helps her reach professional support.

passage:
I sit across from Bhupen in the accounts section, and something changed around the end of the quarter. He used to hum while he worked. Then he stopped. He snapped at the office assistant over sugar in his tea, which I had never seen. He sent the vendor file with last month's figures, twice. At lunch he took his box to his desk instead of the canteen.
In the Monday meeting our manager said, "Bhupen, sleeping on the job?" and a couple of people laughed. Bhupen went red and said nothing.
I didn't know what was going on inside him, and I still don't fully. But that evening I waited till the floor emptied and said, "You've seemed really tired lately. No pressure, but I'm around if you want to talk." He was silent, then said he hadn't slept properly in weeks. I mentioned our company's counselling line and wrote the number on a sticky note. He tucked it into his wallet.
I'm Gautam, by the way. I just thought someone should ask.

qa.q: What did Bhupen send twice?
qa.a: The vendor file with last month's figures.

qa.q: What might Gautam have been feeling while watching the Monday meeting?
qa.a: Gautam was probably uncomfortable and concerned, seeing Bhupen go red while others laughed, and that led to the private check-in that evening.

qa.q: Why did Gautam's check-in work better than the manager's remark?
qa.a: It was private and caring, naming tiredness without blame and offering the counselling line, while the public joke only embarrassed Bhupen.

qa.q: What was the Monday meeting like for Bhupen?
qa.a: It was probably humiliating for Bhupen, who went red and said nothing while people laughed.

grounding: Shows a coworker noticing irritability, careless errors and withdrawal, and choosing a private, caring check-in that points to professional help.
